newsitem.title: ISRAEL: A year on, Peres recalls kiss he gave slain Rabin.
newsitem.headline: A year on, Peres recalls kiss he gave slain Rabin.

text.p: A year after Israeli leader Yitzhak Rabin's assassination, Shimon Peres remembers saying farewell to his dead peace partner that night with a kiss on the forehead.

Hours earlier the two legendary political rivals, who as prime minister and foreign minister together forged peace with the Arabs, had embraced in front of 100,000 cheering Israelis at a Tel Aviv rally.

"In a way these were the happiest hours of his life...He didn't expect to see such a huge gathering and such an enthusiastic public...He was really moved," Peres, 73, told Reuters on Wednesday in an interview to mark the November 4 anniversary.
It was the last time Peres saw Rabin alive. Moments later Rabin was shot and rushed to hospital. Peres arrived later.
"After the head of the hospital told me that Yitzhak is no longer alive, I went to the room where he was lying to say farewell. He was covered with a sheet. It was only his face.
"On the face there was a sort of almost sarcastic smile as if still the happiness goes on. I kissed him on his forehead," Peres said. "I was shocked to my bones."
The rally had special significance at a time when Rabin was being labelled a traitor and a murderer by Israeli protesters opposed to his peace moves.
Rabin, basking in the support, sang out loud for the first time in the 50 years that Peres, the foreign minister, had known him. They sang the Hebrew "Song of Peace."
"They gave us the words of the song and he put it in his pocket, and his heart and the song were penetrated by the same cartridges at the same time," Peres said.

After the rally Israeli gunman Yigal Amir shot Rabin, 73, in the back while the prime minister was striding to his car. Just seconds before, Peres caught a glimpse of Rabin 10 to 12 meters (yards) away.
"I closed the door of my car and then I heard the three shots. I didn't know anything. But my security people became very alarmed. They didn't know what happened and they wouldn't let me go out.
"As you know, it came out that the assassin planned to kill the two of us," Peres said.

Peres's bodyguards kept him at their offices, fearing for his safety. When they learned Rabin was on his way to hospital, Peres threatened to walk there if they wouldn't allow him to go by car. They finally let him go.
At a cabinet meeting that same night Peres became acting prime minister. Israel marks the assassination on Thursday, the anniversary according to the Jewish calendar.

The two Labour party leaders had never been an easy match: Rabin, a gravelly-voiced warrior-turned-peacemaker, and Peres, the perpetual prophet of peace long tagged a dreamer by war-hardened Israelis including Rabin.

"You know we belonged to the same family but it wasn't necessarily a happy family. We used to disagree and to quarrel. There's no sense for me to deny it or ignore it. But when it came to the peace process, we really began to have an agreeable family," Peres said.
At Rabin's funeral, Peres addressed his fallen comrade as his "older brother".
"You know that was the only expression that I didn't have written in my speech that came spontaneously...I felt that he is the senior partner, by age, by position, by responsibility."
Peres insisted that despite his loss to Benjamin Netanyahu in an election five months ago and problems plaguing Middle East peacemaking, Rabin's legacy had been fulfilled.
"His legacy is...that is unfair on our part to charge the younger generation with the dilemmas of peace -- that it was for us and up to us to take the difficult decisions. And that's what we did.
"I am sure that if somebody would come up to him 10 minutes before he was assassinated with a pistol and told him, 'peace or your life', he wouldn't give up peace," Peres said.

"I really miss him. I miss him more than a friend and more than a fellow and more than a human being. I miss him as a partner for probably the most important and potent struggle that our nation is going to face."
